newsitem.title: VIETNAM: Vietnam breaks silence on Deng's death.
newsitem.headline: Vietnam breaks silence on Deng's death.

text.p: Vietnam's communist authorities broke a 12-hour silence on Thursday to report the death of China's paramount leader Deng Xiaoping on state radio.

The news was carried in a brief item on noon bulletins on the same day that at least one official newspaper described Hong Kong reports of Deng's deteriorating health as ill-intentioned attempts to interfere in China's internal affairs.

Thursday's broadcast ended what was becoming a conspicuous silence over Deng's death. There were no signs of anything unusual outside Beijing's embassy and flags throughout the city's main diplomatic quarter remained at full mast.
Analysts said earlier that Deng's death was expected to have few immediate consequences for Hanoi, but added that Vietnam would be scrutinising developments closely.
"They (the Vietnamese government) are well aware, through 4,000 years of history, of what a dynastic succession means," said a Western Vietnam watcher.

"At the moment it looks like Jiang Zemin is in charge, but the military may wish to show its strength at some point. Maybe it will be against Taiwan, maybe against the Spratlys. They (the Vietnamese) will know this."

The Spratlys are a potentially-oil rich series of reefs and islands in the South China Sea, whose sovereignty is claimed in whole or part by a number of regional countries including China and Vietnam.
Most observers said the full impact of Deng's death would depend on the fallout in China, and was therefore unlikely to be known for some time.

But they said a matter of immediate concern for Vietnam -- the recipient in recent years of billions of dollars in Chinese-related foreign investment pledges -- would be the impact on stock markets in Hong Kong, Taipei and Singapore.
Hanoi was not expected to spend much time mourning Deng.

"There will be muted expressions of sorrow, but out of the sides of their faces," said an academic. "Everyone knows that he (Deng) was responsible for all the venom against Vietnam between 1978 and 1985."

The pragmatic reforms that Deng inspired in China swept south into Vietnam in the mid-1980s where they were officially adopted through a home grown version of the policy, known as 'Doi Moi' or renovation.
At that time relations between Hanoi and Beijing were still soured from a bloody border war during the late 1970s and occasional frontier hostilities which were to continue for most of the 1980s.
More than a million people in Vietnam are ethnic Chinese.
Ties are seen as having improved in recent years with a growing number of top-level exchanges between the communist neighbours.
Deng became acquainted with the late president Ho Chi Minh during the 1920s, but the two men are said not to have got on, and he is not known to have visited Vietnam.
